input: Given question: A 38 year old male presents with morning stiffness and pain in lower back/buttocks which improves on exercise. He has has a history of chronic back pain which also sometimes wakes him up during the night. What is the most likely diagnosis? Option A: Spondylosis Option B: Herniates IV disk Option C: Spondylolisthesis Option D: Ankylosing Spondyilitis Option E: Quada Equina Syndrome The correct answer is Option D.
reference: A - Spondylosis - This is a condition which refers to the degenerative osteoarthritis of the joints between the spinal vertebrae/ facet joints. As it progresses the patient does have a stiff back/restricted movement. Pain is worse in the morning and evening BUT is made worse with extended activity B - Herniates IV disk - Usually occurs in the L4/L5 OR L5/S1 vertebrae. Although it usually occurs in men and aged 30-50 the pain is of sudden onset, whilst twisting or lifting heavy objects. Also the pain is usually relieved with lying down flat. C - Spondylolisthesis - Is a complication of spondylosis where there is a defect in the pars interarticularis which makes it become detached. This can then cause the vertebrae to slip out of place. Symptoms include lower back pain when standing or on activity, tenderness, stiffness and tingling radiating down legs. D - Ankylosing spondylitis - The CORRECT answer - The symptoms fit within the classifications which is chronic back pain accompanied with 3/4 of the following - morning stiffness, improvement of pain with exercise, awakening at night because of pain, alternating buttock pain. Is characterised by inflammation of the spine, fusing of the sacroiliac joints which can progress to most of the spine (bamboo spine) and maintained lumbar lordosis in flexion. ALSO usually presents in patients under 50 E - Quada Equina Syndrome - Is caused by compression of the nerves in the cauda equina. Symptoms include 1 or more of the following: bladder dysfunction (urinary retention in 50-70%), reduced sensation in perineal area, sexual dysfunction, neurological defects in the lower limb.

It is a condition in which the inner part of the disk bulges out through the outer part, putting pressure on a nearby nerve. It is most common in the lumbar spine and can be caused by spondylosis, herniated disk, or degenerative conditions. It is not caused by this particular set of symptoms. It occurs when the nerve that runs down the side of the spine (the sciatic nerve) is squeezed or irritated in some way. It is usually caused by something that is wrong with the spine, such as a herniated disk, spondylolisthesis, or degenerative disc disease. Source: 'Imaging the Lower Back' lecture in Case 12. She describes to the GP how after not doing as well as she had hoped in a test, she now believes that she will never get the grades she wants and will never go to uni. Based on this, she has decided not to apply for uni. What is the most likely form of thinking stratergy? Option A: Arbitrary interferences Option B: Black and white thinking Option C: Catastrophising Option D: Personalising Option E: Selective Thinking The correct answer is Option C.
reference: Arbitrary interferences - drawing negative conclusions off the back of insufficient evidenceBlack and white thinking - seeing everything in terms of success or failureCatastrophising - exaggerating a minor setback until it becomes a complete disaster Personalising - taking responsibility and blame for all unpleasant things that happenSelective thinking - focusing on negative details or events whilst ignoring positive ones
best_explanation: Correct answer = C - catastrophising is a form of negative thinking where an individual exaggerates the negative effects of a situation. Arbitrary interferences = this is when an individual adds extra demands or rules which can be disregarded, often in an attempt to reduce anxiety. Black and white thinking = this is when an individual lacks the ability to see the middle ground and tends to see things in extremes. This is also known as 'all or nothing thinking'. Personalising = this is when an individual takes full responsibility for something, even if it is not their fault. Selective thinking = this is when an individual focuses on one aspect of a situation and ignores others. This can be used to either emphasise the negative aspects or to ignore the negative aspects. input: Given question: You are a junior doctor in A and E. You see a wild Asmaf arrive at the hospital with a knife stuck in the left side of his spinal cord. Where would you expect to find a loss? Option A: Contralateral = light touch and proprioception; Ipsilateral = pain, vibration, temperature Option B: Contralateral = vibration, proprioception and 2 touch discrimination; ipsilateral = light touch, pain, temperature Option C: Ipsilateral = vibration, proprioception, motor control ; contralateral = pain, temperature, light touch Option D: Ipsilateral = vibration, proprioception ; contralateral = pain, temperature, light touch, motor control Option E: Contralateral = vibration, pain, motor control; Ipsilateral = temperature, light touch The correct answer is Option C.
reference: C – Only the Lateral Spinothalamic tract crosses over in the spinal cord. So a lesion in the spinal cord will cause CONTRALATERAL loss of pain, temperature and light touch.The DCML (vibration, proprioception), Spinocerebelar (proprioception) and corticospinal (limb motor) cross in the medulla *, so a lesion to the spinal cord will cause loss on the SAME (IPSILATERAL) side, as they nerves have already crossed over.*Apart from Spinocerebelar – doesnt cross, stays on same side.
best_explanation: Knife in the spinal cord = high level lesion  Loss of function expected = loss of vibration, proprioception and motor control  Asmaf is a wild animal, therefore he is likely to have a contralateral loss  As the lesion is high in the spinal cord, loss of pain, temperature and light touch are likely to be ipsilateral  Note: 2 touch discrimination = ability to distinguish between 2 different textures  Light touch = crude touch, vibration, proprioception, 2 touch discrimination  Pain, temperature = somatic afferent fibres  Motor = efferent fibres  Proprioception = interoreceptors, crude touch, vibration, 2 touch discrimination  Discriminative touch = vibration, proprioception, motor control  Nociceptive = pain, temperature  Crude touch = light touch, 2 touch discrimination, pressure  Vibration = light touch, proprioception, discriminative touch  Temperature = nociceptive, crude touch  In this question, the loss of vibration, proprioception and motor control would all be ipsilateral as they are all part of the dorsal column pathway  The loss of pain and temperature would be contralateral as they are both part of the spinothalamic pathway  The light touch and 2 touch discrimination would be contralateral as they are both part of the dorsal column pathway  The crude touch, proprioception and vibration would be ipsilateral as they are all part of the dorsal column pathway  Note: The dorsal column pathway crosses over at the spinal cord level, therefore lesions above or below the spinal cord will result in contralateral or ipsilateral loss respectively  The spinothalamic pathway does not cross over, therefore lesions in this pathway will result in ipsilateral loss  Sources: Dr McCarthy Cord Syndrome Tutorial and Mr McCarthy's spinal cord lecture in case 13  Cord Syndrome: This is a rare syndrome which occurs when blood supply to the spinal cord is lost (usually as a complication of surgery). The affected area of the spinal cord becomes compressed and there is loss

instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: A 27-year-old woman presents with amenorrhoea, and a subsequent pregnancy test gives a positive result. She takes a lithium-based drug to treat her schizophrenia; lithium is known to have teratogenic effects such as inhibiting the formation of new blood vessels from endothelial cells in the embryo. Which process, described above, is inhibited by lithium? Option A: Angiogenesis Option B: Arborisation Option C: Haematopoiesis Option D: Somatogenesis Option E: Vasculogenesis The correct answer is Option E.
reference: Angiogenesis - Formation of new blood vessels from the sprouting of new capillaries from pre-existing vessels.Arborisation - 'Branching out' of a structure such as a nerve fibre or blood vessel. In the embryo, placental capillaries arborise to increase the blood and nutrient supply to the developing foetus.Haematopoiesis - Formation of new blood cells.Somatogenesis - The process of somite formation. Somites differentiate to specialise into different cell types depending on their location.Vasculogenesis - De novo development of blood vessels from endothelial cells differentiating in situ. Key to the provision of nutrition to the foetus. Angiogenesis and vasculogenesis may be confused with one another. Vasculogenesis comes first and occurs in utero, whereas angiogenesis occurs across one's lifetime - angiogenic disease processes include retinopathy and tumour vascularisation. In this question, vasculogenesis is correct as the stem refers to de novo formation from endothelial cells. From Dave Wilson's lecture on 'Embryology of the Cardiovascular System' in Case 8. I used lithium as a clinical stem for this embryology question, but here's the link to the paper I used if you're interested - https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16611133
best_explanation: A = incorrect as this is the process of new blood vessel formation from pre-existing vessels B = incorrect as this is the process by which endothelial cells spread out and become more specialised to form blood vessels C = incorrect as this is the process of generating all the blood cells, including erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets D = incorrect as this is the process of forming all the tissues and organs E = correct as lithium inhibits vasculogenesis; the formation of new blood vessels from endothelial cells. Source: Dave Wilson's lecture on congenital malformations and teratology.

Source: Dave Wilson's lecture on congenital malformations and teratology.

input: Given question: Which of the following is not a cause of Addison's disease? Option A: Tuberculosis Option B: Type 2 Diabetes Option C: Sarcoidosis Option D: Metastatic cancer Option E: Haemochromatosis The correct answer is Option B.
reference: Addison's disease is primary hypoadrenalism i.e. decreased production of the hormones produced by the adrenal glands e.g. cortisol, aldosterone. It is a result of damage or pathology of the adrenal gland. A) Tuberculosis causes granulomas to form in the adrenal gland resulting in the necrosis of the cortex > Addison's.B) Type 2 diabetes does not cause Addison's. However, those with autoimmune diseases such as Type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia and thyroiditis may also have Addison's disease due to autoimmune destruction of the adrenal gland which causes them to shrink.C) Sarcoidosis causes granulomas to form in the adrenal gland  > Addison's D) Cancer (esp. breast cancer) can metastasise to the adrenal glands causing them to increase in size, this interferes with the architecture of the gland meaning they cannot secrete the adrenal hormones > Addison's E) Haemachromatosis is the accumulation of iron in the adrenal gland > Addison's Other causes include:Fungal infection - granulomas form in adrenal glandSystemic amyloidoisis - amyloid protein builds up in the adrenal glandsCase: Endocrine Overview Lecture
best_explanation: Tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis, and metastatic cancer all cause Addison's disease.  Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a cause of Type 2 diabetes mellitus, but is not a cause of Addison's disease.  Addison's disease is caused by destruction of the adrenal cortex, leading to primary hypoadrenalism.  This can be due to:  Tuberculosis  Sarcoidosis  Haemochromatosis  Metastatic cancer  Type 2 diabetes mellitus Destruction of the adrenal medulla, leading to secondary hypoadrenalism, can be due to:  Cushing's syndrome  Pheochromocytoma  Hyperaldosteronism  Hypocortisol  Hypothyroidism  Chronic stress  (Note that destruction of the adrenal medulla is not the same as damage to the adrenal cortex, and that destruction of the adrenal cortex is not the same as damage to the adrenal medulla.  Both the cortex and the medulla can be damaged, and damage to either can lead to hypoadrenalism.)
